title: From inertial postulates to spacetime geometry
body:
This module begins with the measurements made in inertial frames and two physical postulates: equal standing for those frames and a common vacuum light speed. With explicit assumptions about homogeneity, spatial isotropy and common calibration, we can use these inputs to work out the Lorentz boost.
We then ask which measuring rule the boosts preserve. This determines the Minkowski bilinear form up to an overall scale; applying that metric to a pair of events gives their interval. Keeping this order makes the reasoning easier to follow and avoids using the interval to justify the very metric that defines it.
Clock-rate comparisons, length measurements, light cones and spacetime diagrams put this structure to work. In each case, choosing the events carefully helps explain the result. The module also distinguishes a field law's local dependence from the further requirement that its signals propagate causally. Along the way, it is worth noticing what each claim does: some define our terms, some state physical postulates or conventions, and others are results we derive from those inputs.
statement: Inertial postulates determine boosts; their invariant geometry explains intervals, clock rates and lengths.

title: From travelling clocks to rest energy
body:
This module follows a particle through spacetime, beginning with the time recorded by its own clock. Proper time and the four-vector transformation rule let us construct position differences and four-velocity without choosing a preferred inertial frame.
Four-momentum then adds dynamics to this geometry. Multiplying four-velocity by mass gives the component pattern, while work, the Newtonian limit and conservation in interactions identify the physical energy and momentum. These inputs must be stated rather than hidden in the notation.
The final concept asks why a resting system can have energy and why retained energy contributes to inertia. A compact four-momentum derivation establishes rest energy, while equal light pulses make the change-of-inertia argument tangible. Heated boxes, trapped radiation and binding illustrate why system boundaries matter and why invariant mass is not simply a count of massive constituents.
statement: Proper time builds four-velocity; physical energy–momentum and conservation connect inertia with rest energy.

title: From chosen actions to local dynamics
body:
This module separates the physical choice of an action from the mathematical procedure used to vary it. The same fixed-boundary reasoning turns whole-path stationarity into the local Euler–Lagrange equations.
Canonical momentum appears in the endpoint variation and permits a regular change from velocity variables to phase space. Hamilton’s equations combine that change of variables with the Euler–Lagrange dynamics; they do not supply a different force law.
Fields extend the method from coordinates along a path to values at every event. Scalar and vector transformation rules specify the kind of variable, while the chosen local Lagrangian density supplies the dynamics. The field variation then prepares the electromagnetic action, symmetry and conservation arguments in later modules.
statement: A Lagrangian specifies a model; stationary variation yields particle and field equations and their Hamiltonian description.

title: Field strength, charge response and electromagnetic energy
body:
This module fixes one SI potential and tensor convention, then uses it consistently to recover electric and magnetic fields. Their observer-dependent split is tied to the Lorentz transformation of one field strength, not to separate relativistic substances.
Gauge freedom distinguishes redundant potential changes from physical changes and guides, without uniquely determining, interaction choices. The minimally coupled action is varied explicitly to obtain the external Lorentz force and its power transfer.
The physical electromagnetic stress–energy tensor then connects stored energy, Poynting flux, momentum density and stress. Component extraction retains the SI factors and the vacuum scope. Gauge fixing, including the Lorenz condition, simplifies representation without adding field dynamics or concealing residual freedom.
statement: Potentials construct field strength; a consistent coupling yields force, and the Maxwell action supplies field energy–momentum.

title: Symmetry, sources and propagating field energy
body:
This module develops the local conservation arguments rather than treating conserved quantities as separate slogans. Noether’s current comes from a variational symmetry and the field equations; spacetime translations then construct the canonical energy–momentum tensor.
Charge density and current transform together, but their conservation is a further condition. The Maxwell action supplies a sourced field equation, while the potential construction supplies its homogeneous partner. Their combination explains charge compatibility, Lorenz-gauge wave propagation and the transverse vacuum plane wave.
Finally, the energy–momentum carried by fields must be included when a charge radiates. The account distinguishes necessary conservation balance from the additional modelling needed for a self-force law, including near-field storage, point-particle difficulties and controlled approximations.
statement: Action symmetry gives currents; Maxwell dynamics links compatible sources to waves and energy–momentum exchange.
